(I)
QUESTION PRESENTED
Did the Veterans’ Judicial Review Act strip district courts of
the jurisdiction, recognized by this Court in Johnson v. Robison,
415 U.S. 361 (1974), to hear challenges to the constitutionality of
acts of Congress affecting veterans’ benefits?

(1)

INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE*
Amici curiae are national veterans ’ organizations.
Founded in 1981, the National Veterans Legal Services
Program (“NVLSP”) is a nonprofit organization that
works to ensure that the nation’s 18 million veterans and
active-duty service members have access to benefits for
veterans.  NVLSP does so in part by serving as a national
support center that recruits, trains, and assists thousands
of volunteer lawyers and veterans’ advocates.  For over
two decades, NVLSP has published the 2,400 -page
Veterans Benefits Ma nual, the leading practice guide on
the subject.
The Secretary of the Department of Veterans Affairs
(“VA”) has recognized NVLSP as a n organization
authorized to assist veterans in the preparation,
presentation, and prosecution of their benefits claims.  See
38 U.S.C. § 5902.  NVLSP has represented thousands of
veterans in proceedings before the VA , the Board of
Veterans’ Appeals (“Board” or “BVA”), and the Court of
Appeals for Veterans Claims (“Veterans Court”  or
“CAVC”).  NVLSP also has filed numerous amicus briefs
in this Court (and others) in cases that present issues of
broad importance to veterans and the VA benefits system.
Amicus Connecticut Veterans Legal Center
(“CVLC”) provides legal representation at no cost to lowincome veterans and is the creator of the nation’s first
medical legal partnership co -located with the VA.
CVLC’s mission is to empower, support, and improve the

*No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in part, and
no person or entity other than amic i and their counsel made a
monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation or
submission of this brief.   Counsel of record were provided notice of
amici’s intent to file this brief in compliance with Supreme Court Rule
37.2.

2


lives of Connecticut veterans by providing free legal
assistance to help them overcome barriers to housing,
healthcare, income, and recovery.   As part of this work,
CVLC attorneys assist veterans in VA service -connected
disability claims and in applications to correct military
records made to the Department of Defense ( “DoD”).
CVLC advocates for policy changes to create a more
inclusive veterans benefits system for the most vulnerable
low-income veterans: those who are living with mental
illness, trauma, substance dependence, and homelessness
as a result of their service, those who have experienced
military sexual trauma, and those who have been harmed
by discrimination or other injustices in the DoD and VA
systems.
 Amicus Swords to Plowshares is a community-based
not-for-profit organization in San Francisco providing
needs assessment and case management, employment
and training, housing, and legal assistance to veterans —
particularly veterans who are low -income, experiencin g
housing insecurity, and living with mental health
conditions.  Swords to Plowshares promotes and protects
the rights of veterans through advocacy, public education,
and partnership with local, state, and national entities, as
well as direct repres entation of veterans before the VA
and other government agencies.  In its legal work, Swords
to Plowshares assists hundreds of veterans each year at
every level of the VA adjudicatory system to obtain both
monetary disability benefits and access to healthcare.
As Petitioner explains, the text of the Veterans’
Judicial Review Act (“VJRA” or “Act”)  demonstrates
Congress did not preclude district courts from hearing
facial constitutional challenges to federal statutes.  Amici
submit this brief to emphasize that the statutory and
legislative history of the VJRA confirms the same

3


conclusion.  Congress designed the VJRA to retain
veterans’ access to district courts for facial constitutional
challenges, exclusively channeling challenges to certain
“decision[s] of the [Secretary]” to the Veterans Court and
the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal
Circuit under the VJRA.  Pub. L. No. 100-697, § 101(a)(1);
§ 223(c), 102 Stat. 4105 (1988) (codified, as amended, in
various sections of 38 U.S.C.).2
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
This Petition raises an important question of
statutory interpretation that courts have struggled with
and which will have profound effects  on the lives of
veterans across the nation:  whether the VJRA stripped
federal district courts of jurisdiction to hear facial
challenges to the constitutionality of veterans’ benefits
legislation.3  In the decision below, the Eleventh Circuit
erroneously construed the VJRA as eliminating district -
court jurisdiction over such challenges .  Johnson v.
United States Cong., 151 F.4th 1287 (11th Cir. 2025).  This
Court should grant certiorari to correct the erroneous
decision below and establish much -needed uniformity,
certainty, and fairness in courts’ consideration of
challenges to the constitutionality of laws  affecting
veterans’ benefits.
As Petitioner explains, Pet. 21-26, the plain text of 38

2 For ease of reference, decisions by the Administrator, and later by
the Secretary following the elevation of the Veterans Administration
to Cabinet status, are referred to as “decisions by the VA.”
3 Consistent with the Petition, amici use the term “facial”
constitutional challenges to refer to claims attacking “ the validity of
a statute based on its inherent characteristics, not as a result of  how
the statute has been applied.”  Elgin v. Dep’t of Treasury, 567 U.S. 1,
35 (2012) (Alito, J., dissenting).

4


U.S.C. § 511(a) makes clear that federal district courts
retain jurisdiction over facial challenges.  And as amici
explain below, the statutory and legislative history of the
VJRA are equally unambiguous.  Congress enacted the
VJRA to provide judicial review of benefits decisions from
the Board of Veterans’ Appeals  (“BVA”), not to curtail
judicial review over constitutional challenges to veterans’
benefits statutes.  Indeed, the VJRA specifically created
the Veterans Court to “ensure that our Nation’s veterans
receive their day in Court. ”  Jefferson v. Collins, No. 24-
4929, 2025 WL 1874677, at *1 (Vet. App. July 8, 2025).
1.  Following World War II and culminating after the
Vietnam War, a highly contested movement for judicial
review of individualized benefit s decisions began.  This
movement was motivated at least in part by veterans
inconsistent access to courts.  In 1974, i n Johnson v.
Robison, 415 U.S. 361 (1974), this Court unanimously held
that Congress had not barred federal courts from
deciding the constitutionality of veterans’ benefits
legislation in 38 U.S. C. § 211, which the Court
distinguished from benefits decisions by the VA.
In the wake of  Robison, courts disagreed about
whether their jurisdiction also extended to challenges
regarding VA regulations or VA procedures.  Then, in
April 1988, months before the VJRA was passed, this
Court issued its decision in Traynor v. Turnage, 485 U.S.
535 (1988), holding that the no-review clause formerly
codified at Section 211 did not preclude review of whether
a VA regulation was inconsistent with a statute applicable
to all federal agencies —a decision that  faced skepticism
from Congress , unlike Robison.  Ultimately, Congress
passed the  VJRA, which established judicial review for
BVA decisions in the newly created Veterans Court, and
on further appeal, the Federal Circuit.

5


2. Congress amended Section 211 when it passed the
VJRA, but it preserved the pertinent language that this
Court interpreted in Robison as permitting district court
review of “actions challenging the constitutionality of laws
providing benefits for veterans.”  Robison, 415 U.S. at
373.  The no -review clause, now  codified at 38 U.S. C.
§ 511(a), like Section 211, applies only to a “decision by”
the VA made “under” a law that affects the provision of
benefits.4  Where “ judicial interpretations have settled
the meaning of an existing statutory provision, repetition
of the same language in a new statute indicates, as a
general matter, the intent to incorporate its  . . . judicial
interpretations as well.”  Bragdon v. Abbott, 524 U.S. 624,
645 (1998).  The legislative history of the VJRA confirms
that Congress ratified this Court’s interpretation in
Robison—namely, that a “decision by” the VA “under” a
statute or pursuant to a VA rule or regulation is distinct
from a “ constitutional challenge  . . . to a decision of
Congress.”  Robison, 415 U.S. at 367.
3. The Eighth and Eleventh Circuits have
misinterpreted the Act and effectively disregarded
Congress’s ratification of Robison, stripping veterans of a
forum that Congress and the Constitution intended
veterans to be able to access.  After the decision below,
only this Court can ensure uniformity in veterans’ rights
to challenge the validity of veterans’ benefits legislation.
ARGUMENT
I. The VJRA Established Judicial Review for Individual
Veterans’ Benefit s Decisions Without Curtailing

4 The former 38 U.S.C. § 211(a) referred to laws “providing benefits
for veterans,” whereas the VJRA refers to laws “affect[ing] the
provision of benefits.”  Robison, 415 U.S. at 367; 38 U.S.C. §  511(a).
This amendment does not affect the central holding of Robison.

6


Judicial Review of Constitutional Challenges to
Statutes.
A. Prior to the VJRA, Congress Prohibited Judicial
Review of Decisions by the VA —But Not of
Congress’s Decisions.
1. In 1930, President Herbert Hoover established the
Veterans Administration (the agency that preceded the
United States Department of Veterans Affairs ) to
coordinate federal veterans’ benefits programs to support
the growing number of veterans following World War I.
Exec. Order No. 5398; Pub. L. No. 71-536, 46 Stat. 1016
(1930).5  In these early years, the VA operated in
“splendid isolation,” generally unconstrained by judicial
review due to what this Court has described as no-review
statutes prohibiting review of individual benefit s
determinations by the VA.  Brown v. Gardner , 513 U.S.
115, 122 (1994) (citing H.R. Rep. No. 100 -963 at 10 (1988)
(“House Report”)).  Indeed, the BVA, an administrative
body within the VA, retained “final authority” over claims
for benefits, and the “BVA’s decision [wa]s not subject to
judicial review. ”  Walters v. Nat ’l Ass ’n of Radiation
Survivors, 473 U.S. 305, 307, 308- 11 (1985) (outlining
administrative scheme).
Although Congress modified these “no-review
clauses” over the years, it  retained a consistent focus on
insulating decisions by the VA  from review .  See infra
Appendix A.  As this Court recognized in Robison, neither
the text nor the primary purposes of the no-review clauses
“suggest[ed] any congressional intent to preclude judicial
cognizance of constitutional challenges to veterans’

5 Given that the Department of Veterans Affairs was the successor to
the original Veterans Administration, amici refer to them both as,
simply, the “VA.”

7


benefits legislation.”  Robison, 415 U.S. at 373.
2. Beginning in  the 1970s, some veterans ’ services
organizations (“VSOs”) —key players in representing
veterans in legislative advocacy before the federal
government and in representing veterans in the benefit s
adjudication process —became increasingly concerned
with the absence of judicial review for benefits
determinations.  Laurence R. Helfer, The Politics of
Judicial Structure: Creating the United States Court of
Veterans Appeals , 25 Conn. L. Rev . 155, 156 (1992)
(discussing the influence of VSOs from World War II to
passage of the VJRA); James D. Ridgway, The Veterans’
Judicial Review Act Twenty Years Later: Confronting
the New Complexities of the Veterans Benefit System, 66
NYU Ann. Surv. of Am. L. 251, 254-55 (2010) (describing
how the VA battled significant calls for judicial review
well before the VJRA).
Other VSOs , along with  the VA and the House
Committee on Veterans’ Affairs (“House Committee”)
opposed judicial review of individualized claims, citing
concerns regarding expertise and capacity.   These
stakeholders viewed the non -adversarial system for
resolving disputes as beneficial  to veterans.   James D.
Ridgway, The Splendid Isolation Revisited: Lessons
from the History of Veterans ’ Benefits Before Judicial
Review, 3 Veterans L. Rev. 135, 216 (2011).  This
disagreement set off a multi-year debate within Congress
over whether to establish  judicial review for VA benefits
determinations.  See 134 Cong. Rec. 31461 (1988)
(statement of Sen. Murkows ki) (“ After working on this
legislation for over 10 years —during which the Senate
has passed judicial review legislation five times —I am
delighted that the dedication and hard work of all those
involved have at last resulted in a consensus on how to

8


proceed.”).
Yet even as Congress considered whether to provide
judicial review of benefits decisions, federal courts
continued to hear facial constitutional challenges.  See,
e.g., Ziviak v. United States, 411 F. Supp. 416, 419 (D.
Mass. 1976) (reviewing challenge to the constitutionality
of 38 U.S.C. §  3203 concerning VA benefits for
hospitalized veterans), aff’d, 429 U.S. 801 (1976)); Horton
v. Roudebush , 411 F. Supp. 529, 530 (N.D. Ga. 1976)
(reviewing constitutional challenge to 38 U.S.C. §  101(4)
concerning definition of “child”); see also  Anderson v.
Veterans Admin., 559 F.2d 935, 937 (5th Cir. 1977)
(recognizing § 211(a) as limiting jurisdiction to
constitutional challenges to statutes).
Some federal courts also exercised jurisdiction over
challenges to VA rules and regulations.  In Wayne State
University v. Cleland, for example, the Sixth Circuit held
that Section 211, as construed in Robison, did not
preclude challenges to the VA’s authority to promulgate
regulations.  590 F.2d 627,  631 (6th Cir. 1978) ; see also
Merged Area X (Educ .) v. Cleland , 604 F.2d 1075, 1078
(8th Cir. 1979) (following Wayne State and hearing
challenge to VA regulation); Univ. of Maryland v.
Cleland, 621 F.2d 98, 101 (4th Cir. 1980) (same);
Evergreen State Coll. v. Cleland, 621 F.2d 1002, 1008 (9th
Cir. 1980) (same); see also Marozsan v. United States, 852
F.2d 1469, 1472 (7th Cir. 1988) (hearing challenge to VA
procedures).  And in April 1988, shortly before the VJRA
was passed, this Court issued its decision in Traynor v.
Turnage, holding that Section 211 did not preclude review
of whether a VA regulation violated a statute applicable
to all federal agencies.  485 U.S. 535, 536 (1988).

9


B. The VJRA Provided Judicial Review for Acts by
the VA—the Act Did Not Preclude District Court
Review of Facial Constitutional Claims.
In 1988, Congress resolved the longstanding debate
over the appropriate amount of judicial review by passing
the VJRA.  C onsistent with the precursor no -review
clauses, Section 511 of the VJRA prohibits judicial review
of “ a decision by the” VA  (i.e., benefits determinations
based on case-specific facts).  As Petitioner explains, that
restriction does not mean that veterans are barred from
challenging the validity of veterans’ benefit statutes ,
which are decisions by Congress, in federal district courts.
Indeed, the legislative history of the VJRA shows that
review in federal district court s was a right to which no
stakeholders objected.  Insofar as members of Congress
or others expressed concerns, it  pertained to courts’
subsequent expansion  of Robison and the resulting
inconsistency amongst courts as to the scope of Section
211 with respect to VA regulations.
1.  The drafting and legislative history of the VJRA—
specifically the competing bills considered alongside the
Act—reveal that Congress considered and rejected
proposals to expand Robison.  Congress instead chose  to
enact the VJRA and  provide a carefully calibrated
structure of judicial review for decisions by the VA (i.e.,
its benefit s decisions and rules and regulations).
Congress did so without abrogating Robison.
In the 100th Congress alone, five comprehensive
veterans’ benefits bills were introduced by members of
the Senate and House Committees on Veterans’ Affairs
that addressed judicial review: Senate Bill 11 (Cranston),
House Bill 639 (Evans), Senate Bill 2992 (Murkowski),
House Bill 5039 (Montgomery), and House Bill 5228
(Montgomery).  Ultimately,  following “intensive

10


negotiations” between the Chairmen and members of the
Committees on Veterans’ Affairs, Congress enacted the
VJRA by passing Senate Bill 11, as modified by Senate
Amendment 3726 (S. Am end. 3726, 100th Cong. (1988)).
See 134 Cong. Rec. 31481 (statement of Sen. Murkowsi).
An Explanatory Statement “prepared by the two
Veterans’ Affairs Committees”  was published in  the
Congressional Record  shortly before the VJRA’s
passage.  See id.  at 31468.  It  reflects the unified
congressional view on the intended scope of judicial
review and the corresponding limits of its preclusion
provision.  See id . at 31473-81 (outlining the Senate
proposal (S. 11), the House Amendment (H.R. 5288), and
the “compromise agreement”).  The Statement
demonstrates that Congress intended to “provid[e] for
judicial review of BVA decisions on the record, and of VA
rules and regulations challenged in the course of a case ”
by the Veterans Court, “ with limited appellate review in
the [Federal Circuit] .”  Id . at 31477 (summarizing Title
III of the VJRA).  Congress believed “[r]eview of VA rules
and regulations on their face, and the process by which
they were issued, would be available in the CAFC under
[Chapter 72]  as well as through direct appeal to the
CAFC.”  Id. 6  The Statement does not evince any
congressional intent for facial constitutional claims to
similarly be subject to review exclusively in the F ederal
Circuit.7

6 Chapter 72 provides the framework for the Veterans Court.  See 38
U.S.C. §§ 7251-7299.
7 Rather, the compromise agreement vested the Federal Circuit with
jurisdiction over a veteran’s challenge to the validity of a statute only
if the statute “was germane to his claim,” (i.e., it contemplated a claim
before the VA).  Id. at 31482.

11


2.  The VJRA’s extensive legislative record likewise
does not  reveal any congressional intent to  abrogate
Robison; instead, the record confirms that Congress
meticulously tailored its new review framework to
address expansions of Robison while leaving undisturbed
the existing path for statutory constitutional challenges.
In fact, the House and Senate Veterans’ Affairs
Committee members who negotiated the VJRA
reaffirmed Robison.  The Chairman of the House
Committee, Sonny Montgomery of Mississippi, explicitly
embraced this Court’s decision in Robison in a 71 -page
report on the House Amendment:
The Supreme Court properly decided that a
decision not to provide benefits to
conscientious objectors was a decision of the
Congress, not of the Administrator, and the
Court was free to examine the
constitutionality of Congress’ decisions . . ..
The result in Johnson v. Robison is
generally accepted as being in accord with a
line of decisions stretching back to Marbury
v. Madison which hold that the courts have
a constitutional responsibility to determine
whether Congressional enactments meet
constitutional muster.
House Report at 19-20 (citing Robison, 415 U.S. at 367).
Indeed, debate over the proper scope of judicial
review never questioned whether claims of constitutional
violations properly belong in district court.  Disabled
American Veterans (“DAV”), comprised of over 1 million
members and accounting for 40% of veterans submitting
claims in 1985,  viewed the non -adversarial process as
consistent with fundamental due process rights in part

12


because “veterans have always been able to take to court
. . . constitutional violations.”  H.R. 585 and Other Bills
Relating to Judicial Review of Veterans Claims: Hrg.
Before the House Comm. on Veterans’ Affs. , 99th Cong.,
Vol. 1, 283-84, 290 (1986) (“H. Hrg. 99-52”).  The General
Counsel for the VA, Donald Ivers, similarly endorsed
Robison’s interpretation of Section 211 as permitting
judicial review of constitutional challenges to veterans’
benefits legislation.  Judicial Review of Veterans’ Affairs:
Hrg. Before the H. Comm. on Veterans’ Affs., 100th Cong.
451 (1988) (“H. Hrg. 100-60”).  Mr. Ivers represented that,
from a policy perspective, the VA would not object to
expanding the exception “to authorize bona fide
challenges to VA regulations” because the VA’s “principal
concern” was “with judicial review of VA benefit decisions
in the Federal courts.”  Id. at 450-52.
The Judicial Conference , which makes
recommendations to Congress concerning legislation
involving the federal judiciary,  expressed similar views.
See H. Hrg. 99 -52, at  31 (testifying that the Judicial
Conference believed “judicial review should be limited to
the review of constitutional issues and statutory
interpretations, including the review of regulations, to see
if they are beyond the authority of the agency to make ”
and opposed “ any provision requiring judicial review of
any factual determination of the V[A].”).
3.  Although Congress and stakeholders unanimously
endorsed Robison, the record shows the Committee
members who negotiated the VJRA viewed as
problematic courts’ reliance on Robison in interpreting
Section 211 to permit review of VA regulations.
Congressman Montgomery expressed concern that
courts paid “too much attention to the policy behind the
enactment of 211(a) as articulated by the Court in

13


Johnson v. Robison, and not enough attention to the
explicit language that Congress used in isolating
decisions of the Administrator  from judicial scrutiny.”
House Report at 22 (emphasis added).
Senator Cranston viewed the VJRA as an opportunity
to clarify the scope of the no -review clause following this
Court’s decision in Traynor , which he believed left
unresolved “ some important differences between the
various U.S. Courts of Appeals regarding the sweep of
this prohibition, particularly with regard to review of
regulations.”  Judicial Review Legislation: Hrg. Before
the S. Comm. on Veterans’ Affs.  on S.11, the Proposed
Veterans’ Administration Adjudication Procedure and
Judicial Review Act, and S. 2992, Veterans’ Judicial
Review Act, 100 Cong. 7 (1988); see also H. Hrg. 100-60 at
451-52 (summarizing circuit split).  Congressman
Montgomery proposed swapping the language “ under
any law administered by” the VA in Section 211 with
“under a law affecting the provisions of benefits.”  House
Report at 27.  He described the substantive effects of the
amendment as precluding district court review of
challenges to either  the validity of: (1) a VA regulation
(reviewed in Wayne State); or (2) the VA’s interpretation
of a VA regulation as consistent with a statute applicable
to all federal agencies (reviewed in Traynor).  Id.
Congressman Montgomery disclaimed any further
substantive effects.  See id.  Accordingly, there is no basis
to infer that Congress made additional substantive
changes—such as precluding judicial review of facial
constitutional challenges to statutes —sub silentio.  See,
e.g., Keene Corp. v. United States, 508 U.S. 200, 209 (1993)
(explaining this Court does not “presume [every]
revision” in a comprehensive revision “worked a change
in the underlying substantive law ‘unless an intent to

14


make such [a] chang[e] is clearly expressed.’”).
The language Congressman Montgomery proposed
was ultimately amended to ensure that “the general
preclusion of judicial review appl[ies] only to a decision by
the [VA],” and codified in the VJRA.  134 Cong. Rec. 31474
(statement of Sen. Murkows ki) (emphasis added). 8
Congress understood that this Court distinguished a
“decision by the VA ” from “a decision of Congress,”
Robison, 415 U.S. at  367; see also  Watson v. United
States, 552 U.S. 74, 82 -83 (2007) (explaining that “long
congressional acquiescence ” of this Court’s
interpretations “‘enhance[s] even the usual precedential
force’ [of this Court’s] interpretation of statutes.”) (citing
Shepard v. United States , 544 U.S. 13, 23 (2005) ).  It
retained that qualifier in the amended no -review clause
precisely because Congress did not intend to abrogate
Robison.
II. The Eleventh Circuit’s Decision Below Is Inconsistent
with the VJRA’s Text and Legislative History.
In the decision below, the Eleventh Circuit
erroneously construed the VJRA as eliminating district -
court jurisdiction over facial constitutional challenges to
veterans’ benefits statutes.  Johnson v. United States
Cong., 151 F.4th 1287, 1289 (11th Cir. 2025) .  In reaching
that conclusion, the Eleventh Circuit focused on the
purported absence of textual support distinguishing facial
claims from as -applied constitutional claims, the Act’s

8 Compare H.R. 5288, 100th Cong. §  2 (1988)  (“The Administrator
shall decide all questions of law and fact necessary to a decision under
a law affecting the provision of benefits”), with VJRA, Pub. L. No.
100-687, § 101(a)(1) (“The Administrator shall decide all questions of
law and fact necessary to a decision by the Administrator under a law
that affects the provision of benefits by the Administrator to
veterans.” (emphases added)).

15


amendments to the no -review clause, and the Federal
Circuit’s exclusive jurisdiction over legal issues reached
by the VA and Veterans Court, including the validity of
veterans’ benefits statutes.  None of those considerations
supports the Eleventh Circuit’ s interpretation of the
VJRA as abrogating Robison.9
First, t he Eleventh Circuit overlook ed the textual
support distinguishing between as -applied and facial
claims: a “decision by the Secretary ” refers to the
Secretary’s “interpretation or application of a . . . statute
[or regulation] to a particular set of facts,” not to facial
challenges to statutes.  Robison, 415 U.S. at 367.
Second, there is no basis for the Eleventh Circuit’s
holding that the amendment to the no-review clause—i.e.,
expanding the clause from insulating review of VA
decisions “under a law administered by” the VA to
insulating review of VA decisions “under a law that
affects” the VA’s provision of benefits —somehow
“foreclosed the very distinction on which Robison rested.”
Johnson, 151 F.4th at 1296.  Section 511, like Section 211,
refers to “a decision by the [VA]” “under” a law.  38 U.S.C.
§ 511(a) (emphasis added).  And “[a] decision of law or fact
‘under’ a statute is made by the [VA] in the interpretation
or application of a particular provision of the statute to a
particular set of facts,” whereas “Appellee’s constitutional
challenge is not to any such decision of the [VA] , but
rather to a decision of Congress . . . .”  Robison, 415 U.S.
at 367.
Finally, the Eleventh Circuit overlooked the
limitations on the Federal Circuit’s jurisdiction over

9 We note that the Eleventh Circuit joins the Eighth Circuit as the
only courts to adopt this view.  See Petition 14.

16


challenges to the validity of veterans’ benefits statutes.
Unlike facial challenges to the VA’s rulemaking authority,
which the Federal Circuit may review in the first instance
under 38 U.S.C. §  502, challenges to the validity of
statutes are only reviewable by the Federal Circuit after
the Veterans Court enters a decision if the Veterans
Court decided the issue.  38 U.S.C. §  7292(a).  The
Eleventh Circuit nonetheless concluded that “Congress’s
intent to exclude district -court jurisdiction [is] ‘fairly
discernible’ from the Act. ”  Johnson, 151 F.4th at  1293
(citing Elgin v. Dep’t of Treasury, 567 U.S. 1, 9-10 (2012))
(alteration in original).
The VJRA’s “text, structure, and purpose” does not
support the view that Congress implicitly abrogated
Robison, a decision unanimously supported by the
VJRA’s chief negotiators and drafters.  Elgin, 567 U.S. at
10.  As we have explained above, the legislative history of
the VJRA and Congress’s  decision to retain the same
language aimed at prohibiting judicial review of only
decisions of law or fact which arise in the context of a
benefits decision indicates the opposite.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the petition for a writ of
certiorari should be granted.

review any such decisions.”
